message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"72e01a6b3ef1f3c35fdfe17ad04b8f2a63acf6b70a2d6563bda5ef3e32e881d3","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-fl-class-e:lineage:69","source_registry_sha256":"b17b1a3691c9724cc739459037987900e5b1edce40443ad13e42b6eee3e12974","units":[{"unit_id":"sec01-u01","module_id":"sec01-m01","objective_ids":["sec01-u01"],"title":{"text":"Residency and who needs licenses","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Knowing whether you count as a Florida resident tells you whether you must carry a Florida license on public roads.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Dana moves to Florida and starts a new job right away.","fact_ids":["sec01-F03","sec01-R01"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Newcomers who work or attend school fall under the thirty-day license clock.","fact_ids":["sec01-R01"]},"result":{"text":"Dana has thirty days to get a Florida license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking an international driving permit lets a visitor drive by itself.","fact_ids":["sec01-R03"]},"correction":{"text":"An international permit works only beside the home-country license.","fact_ids":["sec01-R03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Domicile, vote, or file makes you a resident.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A visitor aged sixteen holds a valid license from their home state. Must they get a Florida license?","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"No, a licensed visitor sixteen or older is excused.","fact_ids":["sec01-R03"]},"rationale":{"text":"A home-state license alone excuses a visitor who is sixteen or older.","fact_ids":["sec01-R03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who needs a Florida license","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Residency and legal status","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03"]},{"text":"Who must carry a Florida license","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson starts with a basic question: who has to carry a Florida driver license? The answer depends on two ideas. The first is residency, which the handbook ties to living here, registering to vote, or filing domicile papers. The second is legal status, because immigrants, non-immigrants and citizens are each defined differently. Once those two ideas are clear, the rules for newcomers and exemptions fall into place. Residents must carry a Florida license whenever they drive on public roads, newcomers who work or go to school here have a short deadline, and some groups are excused entirely.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What makes you a resident","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Domicile here over six straight months","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-R01"]},{"text":"Registering to vote, or filing domicile or homestead papers","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Residency in Florida means one of three things. You have made your home here for more than six months in a row, you have registered to vote here, or you have filed papers declaring domicile or homestead. Any one of these makes you a resident. Notice that residency is about where you live and what you have filed, not about whether you have a job. The thirty-day license clock is a separate rule: it binds newcomers who work or attend school. Keep the two ideas apart, because a question may describe one and quietly ask about the other.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Three kinds of legal status","fact_ids":["sec01-F02","sec01-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Immigrants are lawful permanent residents","fact_ids":["sec01-F02","sec01-R02"]},{"text":"Non-immigrants enter briefly for a stated purpose","fact_ids":["sec01-F02","sec01-R02"]},{"text":"Citizens were born here or naturalized","fact_ids":["sec01-F02","sec01-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"The handbook sorts applicants into three legal statuses. Immigrants are lawful permanent residents, admitted by visa or by an adjustment of status through the federal immigration agency. Non-immigrants enter only for a short time and for a stated purpose. Citizens were either born here or naturalized. These labels matter later, because each status brings its own documents to prove identity. A simple way to hold them is stay, visit or belong: immigrants stay permanently, non-immigrants visit for a purpose, and citizens belong by birth or naturalization.","fact_ids":["sec01-F02","sec01-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Who must carry, who is excused","fact_ids":["sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Residents carry a Florida license on public roads","fact_ids":["sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01"]},{"text":"Working or schooling newcomers have thirty days","fact_ids":["sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01"]},{"text":"Several groups are exempt","fact_ids":["sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Residents must carry a Florida license on public roads. A newcomer who works or goes to school here must get one within thirty days. Several groups are excused: licensed visitors who are sixteen or older, federal crews, military service families and commuters. The handbook adds more exempt groups: college students, migrant workers licensed in their home state, and people who operate a tractor or road machine only briefly. For example, if Dana moves here and starts a job right away, Dana falls under the thirty-day clock and must get a Florida license within that time.","fact_ids":["sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Permits do not stand alone","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"A home-state license alone can excuse a visitor","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},{"text":"An international permit needs the home-country license beside it","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a common trap. A visitor who is sixteen or older and holds a valid license from home is excused from getting a Florida license, and that home license is enough by itself. An international driving permit is different. It works only when it is carried beside the license from the driver's home country. So a visitor who shows only an international permit is not covered by it alone. When a question mentions an international permit, look for the home-country license that has to go with it before you decide the visitor may drive.","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the visitor rule","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"A licensed visitor aged sixteen","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},{"text":"Must they get a Florida license?","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a visitor who is sixteen holds a valid license from their home state and plans to drive here. Must that visitor get a Florida license? Decide before you go on. The answer is no. Licensed visitors who are sixteen or older are on the list of people excused from holding a Florida license, and the home-state license alone covers them. The answer would change if the visitor carried only an international permit, because that permit works only beside a home-country license. A home license and the age of sixteen are the two things to check.","fact_ids":["sec01-R03","sec01-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Residency and exemptions recap","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01","sec01-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Domicile, vote, or file","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01","sec01-R02"]},{"text":"Thirty days for working or schooling newcomers","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01","sec01-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, residency comes from making your home here for more than six months, registering to vote, or filing domicile or homestead papers. Immigrants are lawful permanent residents, non-immigrants visit briefly for a purpose, and citizens were born here or naturalized. Residents carry a Florida license on public roads, and newcomers who work or attend school have thirty days to get one. Licensed visitors sixteen and older, federal crews, service families, commuters, college students, home-licensed migrant workers and brief machine operators are excused.","fact_ids":["sec01-F01","sec01-F02","sec01-F03","sec01-F04","sec01-R01","sec01-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec01-u02","module_id":"sec01-m02","objective_ids":["sec01-u02"],"title":{"text":"License transfers and classes","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Knowing which outside licenses waive Florida exams, and where Class E ends, saves a new resident from surprises at the office.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R05"]},{"text":"A Class E driver who moves up to a larger motorcycle needs an endorsement, so the class rules matter day to day.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lena moves from Germany with a valid German license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05"]},"reasoning":{"text":"German licenses waive the skills exam only, and vision still applies.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},"result":{"text":"Lena still needs the vision screening and the knowledge exam, but not the skills exam.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking every foreign license waives both Class E exams.","fact_ids":["sec01-R04"]},"correction":{"text":"Most listed licenses waive both exams, but German ones waive only the skills exam and kept Canadian cards force testing.","fact_ids":["sec01-R04","sec01-F05"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Class E stops below the commercial line.","fact_ids":["sec01-R05"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A driver wants to ride a motorcycle over fifty cubic centimeters on a Class E license. What else is needed?","fact_ids":["sec01-F06"]},"answer":{"text":"A motorcycle endorsement.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Class E covers non-commercial vehicles, and motorcycles over fifty cubic centimeters need an endorsement.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Transfers and license classes","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Outside licenses that waive exams","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},{"text":"Class E versus commercial","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"New residents often arrive with a license from somewhere else. This lesson explains when that license lets you skip Florida's Class E exams, and when it does not. Then we draw the line between the ordinary Class E license and the commercial licenses that govern heavy rigs, large passenger carriers and placarded hazardous cargo. Along the way you will see the motorcycle endorsement, which a Class E driver needs for larger motorcycles. These rules are short, but the exceptions are exactly what exam questions like to test.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Licenses that waive exams","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Listed states, Canada, France, Taiwan and Korea waive both exams","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},{"text":"German licenses waive skills only","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},{"text":"Vision still applies","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"A valid license from a listed state, or from Canada, France, Taiwan or Korea, waives both Class E exams, the knowledge exam and the skills exam. German licenses are treated differently: they waive the skills exam only. In every case the vision check still applies. There is also a catch for Canadian drivers. If you keep your Canadian card instead of surrendering it, you must take the tests. So think of three outcomes: both exams waived for most listed licenses, skills only for Germany, and full testing when a Canadian card is kept.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Worked example: a German license","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Lena arrives with a German license","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},{"text":"Skills exam waived, vision still applies","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a worked example. Lena moves to Florida with a valid German license. Because German licenses waive only the skills exam, Lena does not take the driving skills test. She still faces the vision check, which applies to everyone, and the knowledge exam is not waived for German licenses. Compare that with a driver arriving from France or Korea, whose valid license waives both Class E exams. If Lena had come from Canada and kept her Canadian card, she would have to take the tests instead. The vision check applies here too, as it does for every outside license.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Where Class E ends","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Class E: non-commercial vehicles under twenty-six thousand one pounds","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R05"]},{"text":"Motorcycles over fifty cubic centimeters need an endorsement","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R05"]},{"text":"Commercial: heavy rigs, sixteen passengers, placarded hazmat","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Class E is the ordinary license. It covers non-commercial vehicles that weigh less than twenty-six thousand one pounds. A Class E driver who wants to ride a motorcycle larger than fifty cubic centimeters needs a motorcycle endorsement. Commercial licenses take over where Class E stops: rigs of twenty-six thousand one pounds or more, vehicles that carry sixteen or more passengers, and vehicles hauling placarded hazardous materials, which also involves vetting. Any one of those three triggers moves the driver into commercial licensing.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":33,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"A kept Canadian card","fact_ids":["sec01-R04","sec01-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keeping a Canadian card forces testing","fact_ids":["sec01-R04","sec01-F05"]},{"text":"German licenses waive skills only","fact_ids":["sec01-R04","sec01-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two exceptions trip people up. The first is the Canadian license. Canadian licenses are on the list that waives both Class E exams, but a driver who keeps the Canadian card must take the tests instead. The second exception is Germany, where only the skills exam is waived. Put the three outcomes side by side: most listed licenses waive both exams, German licenses waive the skills exam only, and a kept Canadian card means full testing. The vision check applies in every one of these cases, so no outside license skips it.","fact_ids":["sec01-R04","sec01-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the motorcycle rule","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Class E driver, larger motorcycle","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},{"text":"What else is needed?","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver holds a Class E license and wants to ride a motorcycle over fifty cubic centimeters. What else does that driver need? Settle on your answer first. The answer is a motorcycle endorsement. Class E covers non-commercial vehicles under twenty-six thousand one pounds, but motorcycles larger than fifty cubic centimeters need the endorsement added. A commercial license is not the answer, because commercial licenses govern heavy rigs, large passenger carriers and placarded hazardous cargo, not motorcycles.","fact_ids":["sec01-F06","sec01-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":33,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Transfers and classes recap","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R04","sec01-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Both exams, skills only, or full testing","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R04","sec01-R05"]},{"text":"Weight, passengers, or hazmat","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R04","sec01-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, most listed state and foreign licenses, including those from Canada, France, Taiwan and Korea, waive both Class E exams. German licenses waive only the skills exam, the vision check always applies, and keeping a Canadian card forces testing. Class E covers non-commercial vehicles under twenty-six thousand one pounds, with an endorsement for motorcycles over fifty cubic centimeters. Commercial duty begins at twenty-six thousand one pounds, at sixteen passengers, or with placarded hazardous cargo. Any one of those three triggers is enough.","fact_ids":["sec01-F05","sec01-F06","sec01-F07","sec01-R04","sec01-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec01-u03","module_id":"sec01-m03","objective_ids":["sec01-u03"],"title":{"text":"Proving identity and address","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F09","sec01-F10"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Arriving with the right original documents is the difference between leaving with a license and being turned away.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-R06"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sam, a citizen, brings a notarized copy of a birth certificate, a Social Security card and one utility bill.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-R06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Notarized copies fail, and every applicant needs two address documents.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-R09"]},"result":{"text":"Sam must bring an original or certified birth certificate and a second address proof.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-F08"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a notarized copy of a document is as good as the original.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06"]},"correction":{"text":"Originals and certified copies pass, while photocopies and notarized copies fail.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Identity, number, two addresses.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"An applicant brings a notarized copy of their passport. Will it be accepted?","fact_ids":["sec01-R06"]},"answer":{"text":"No, notarized copies fail.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Only originals and certified copies pass.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Your document checklist","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Primary identity, Social Security, address","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-R06"]},{"text":"Originals only","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every license applicant arrives with a set of documents, and this lesson walks through that set piece by piece. You need primary identification, proof of your Social Security number or a secondary item, and two documents that prove your address. All of them must be originals. If your name has changed, a marriage, divorce or court paper links the names. We will also look at how each legal status proves identity, what extra papers some groups add, and the short temporary permit that can bridge a document check. Every document in the set must be an original or a certified copy.","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Primary identity by status","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F10","sec01-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Citizens: birth certificate, passport or card, consular report, naturalization papers","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F10","sec01-R07"]},{"text":"Immigrants: green card, passport stamp, asylum or refugee grant","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F10","sec01-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Primary identification depends on your status. A citizen uses a government birth certificate, a passport or passport card, a consular report, or a certificate of naturalization or citizenship. An immigrant shows a green card, a passport stamp, or a grant of asylum or refugee status. Canadians and non-immigrants show their own parallel papers. These are separate tracks, and the handbook does not let you mix papers from one track with another. Find your status first, then bring the primary document that belongs to that track.","fact_ids":["sec01-F09","sec01-F10","sec01-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Extra papers for some groups","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Students add a school form; exchange visitors add theirs","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R08"]},{"text":"Travel, parole and judge-order papers ride with a passport","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some groups add papers on top of their primary document. Students add their school enrollment form, exchange visitors add their exchange form, and refugees bring extra papers. Travel papers, parole papers and judge-order papers each go together with a passport rather than standing on their own. A non-citizen whose papers need checking may receive a sixty-day temporary permit without a photo while agencies verify them. If that verification of the primary and secondary papers fails, the application is denied. So the temporary permit is a bridge, not a guarantee.","fact_ids":["sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Social Security and secondary items","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Number proof: card, tax forms, full-number paycheck, military ID","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-R09"]},{"text":"No number, or a non-immigrant: one secondary item","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Florida collects and verifies Social Security numbers. You can prove yours with the card itself, a wage or income tax form, a paycheck that shows the full number, or a military identification. Citizens and immigrants who have no number, and all non-immigrants, supply one secondary item instead. The secondary list is long: other licenses, military and school records, birth transcripts, older life insurance policies, draft and voter cards, court papers, foreign identification and weapon permits. Only one secondary item is needed.","fact_ids":["sec01-F13","sec01-F14","sec01-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":32,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Two proofs of address","fact_ids":["sec01-F15","sec01-F16","sec01-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Leases, voter, vehicle or vessel records, statements, utility orders","fact_ids":["sec01-F15","sec01-F16","sec01-R09"]},{"text":"Transcripts, licenses, tax forms, bank and government mail","fact_ids":["sec01-F15","sec01-F16","sec01-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Address proof always takes two papers. Accepted papers include leases, voter, vehicle or vessel records, statements, utility hookup orders, booklets, service or medical cards, and insurance papers. The list continues with school transcripts, professional licenses, tax forms, exchange certificates, shelter letters, mail from banks and government offices, and offender forms. If you live in someone else's home, you also add a letter from your host. Compare this with secondary identification, where one listed item is enough. Address proof is the place where two is the rule.","fact_ids":["sec01-F15","sec01-F16","sec01-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Notarized does not mean accepted","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"A notary stamp does not make a copy acceptable","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R09"]},{"text":"Bring originals or certified copies","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many people assume a notary's stamp turns a copy into an acceptable document. The handbook says the opposite: notarized copies fail, just like photocopies. Only originals and certified copies pass. A second trap is mixing tracks. An immigrant cannot swap in a citizen document, and a citizen cannot use a non-immigrant paper; each status follows its own primary identification track. Finally, remember the count: one secondary item when you have no number, but always two address papers. When in doubt, bring the original document.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the copy rule","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"A notarized passport copy","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-F09"]},{"text":"Accepted or refused?","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: an applicant brings a notarized copy of a passport as primary identification. Will it be accepted? Make your decision before continuing. The answer is no. Notarized copies fail, exactly like photocopies. The applicant needs the original passport or a certified copy. If this applicant were a citizen, other original options would include a government birth certificate, a passport card, a consular report, or a naturalization or citizenship certificate. The same rule applies to every other document in the set, so bring originals or certified copies throughout.","fact_ids":["sec01-R06","sec01-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec01-u03-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Documents recap","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R08","sec01-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Identity, number, two addresses","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R08","sec01-R09"]},{"text":"Originals or certified copies only","fact_ids":["sec01-F08","sec01-F11","sec01-F12","sec01-R06","sec01-R07","sec01-R08","sec01-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"To recap, bring primary identification for your own status track, proof of your Social Security number or one secondary item, and two original address documents. Originals and certified copies pass, photocopies and notarized copies fail, and a court or family paper links any name change.
